dx: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome in a 29-week preterm infant of a diabetic mother
case: A male newborn is delivered by cesarean section at 29 weeks' gestation to a 31-year-old woman with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus. Her hemoglobin A1c was 9.4% (normal less than 5.7) during the pregnancy. She did not receive antenatal corticosteroids. Birth weight is 1450 g. Within 30 minutes of birth, he develops tachypnea, expiratory grunting, nasal flaring, and intercostal retractions. Temperature is 36.6 °C (97.9 °F), pulse is 168/min, respirations are 76/min, and blood pressure is 48/30 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 84%. A chest x-ray shows low lung volumes with diffuse, fine reticulogranular opacities and air bronchograms in both lungs. Diagnosis: neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

questions.stem: In the same unit, an infant delivered at 20 weeks' gestation could not be oxygenated despite full ventilatory support. Which of the following structural features, present in this 29-week infant's lungs and absent at 20 weeks, best explains why he can survive with support?
options: Complete branching of the conducting airways to terminal bronchioles
Mature alveoli subdivided by secondary septa
Capillaries in close contact with thin respiratory epithelium
Cartilage plates and submucosal glands in bronchial walls
approach: Place each gestational age in its stage: 20 weeks is early canalicular; 29 weeks is the saccular stage (about week 26 to birth).
Ask what gas exchange needs: a thin epithelium with capillaries pressed against it.
Pick the feature that first appears near the end of the canalicular stage and is present at 29 weeks.
questions.why: Lung development runs through four stages: pseudoglandular (about weeks 5 to 17, airway branching), canalicular (about weeks 16 to 26, respiratory bronchioles form and capillaries grow in), saccular (about week 26 to birth, terminal sacs form), and alveolar (about week 36 into childhood). Late in the canalicular stage, the airspace lining thins and capillaries bulge against it, forming the first blood-air barrier. That is why survival with support first becomes possible at about weeks 24 to 26. At 20 weeks this barrier is not yet in place, so ventilation cannot oxygenate the blood.
whyNot: The conducting airways finish branching down to the terminal bronchioles by the end of the pseudoglandular stage, about week 16 to 17. The 20-week fetus already had them, so they cannot explain the difference. Conducting airways also do no gas exchange.
Secondary septa and mature alveoli form in the alveolar stage, from about week 36 into childhood. A 29-week infant does not have them yet, so they cannot explain his survival.
Correct.
Bronchial cartilage and glands form from splanchnic mesoderm and endoderm early, during the pseudoglandular stage. They are present at 20 weeks and play no part in gas exchange.

questions.stem: Amniotic fluid obtained 2 days before delivery showed a lecithin to sphingomyelin ratio of 1.2 (mature 2.0 or greater). Which of the following best explains why this result predicted his respiratory distress?
options: Lecithin from type II pneumocytes was still too low relative to sphingomyelin
Sphingomyelin from fetal membranes had risen above its usual late-gestation level
Type I pneumocytes had not yet started secreting lecithin into fetal lung fluid
Fetal kidneys had not yet excreted enough lecithin into the amniotic fluid
approach: Recall where amniotic lecithin comes from: surfactant made by type II pneumocytes, carried out with fetal lung fluid.
Recall that sphingomyelin stays fairly constant and acts as the yardstick.
A ratio under 2 means surfactant output is still immature, which predicts alveolar collapse after birth.
questions.why: Type II pneumocytes begin making surfactant in the second trimester, but output reaches mature levels only at about week 35. Fetal lung fluid carries surfactant into the amniotic fluid, so amniotic lecithin tracks surfactant production. Sphingomyelin changes little, so the lecithin to sphingomyelin ratio rises as the lungs mature. A ratio of 2 or more signals mature lungs. His ratio of 1.2 showed that surfactant was still too low to keep his alveoli open.
whyNot: Correct.
Sphingomyelin stays roughly constant through late gestation and serves as the reference value. The ratio is low because lecithin has not risen, not because sphingomyelin is high.
Type I pneumocytes are thin gas exchange cells and do not make surfactant. Type II pneumocytes make it.
Lecithin in amniotic fluid comes from fetal lung fluid that flows out through the trachea. It is not a kidney product.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how his mother's poorly controlled diabetes increased his risk of this condition?
options: Maternal insulin crossing the placenta and suppressing type II pneumocytes
Fetal hypoglycemia limiting glycerol supply for phospholipid synthesis
Maternal ketoacids crossing the placenta and degrading dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine
Fetal hyperinsulinemia opposing glucocorticoid induction of surfactant synthesis
approach: Trace the glucose: maternal hyperglycemia crosses the placenta and makes the fetus hyperglycemic.
The fetal pancreas responds with high insulin output.
Fetal insulin blunts the cortisol signal that turns on surfactant synthesis in type II pneumocytes.
questions.why: Surfactant is mostly phospholipid, with dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (lecithin) as the main surface-active lipid, plus phosphatidylglycerol and surfactant proteins. Fetal cortisol and thyroid hormone promote its synthesis, which is why antenatal corticosteroids are given before preterm birth. Glucose crosses the placenta but maternal insulin does not, so the fetus of a hyperglycemic mother makes large amounts of its own insulin. Fetal hyperinsulinemia opposes the effect of cortisol and delays surfactant production, so these infants can develop respiratory distress even at gestational ages that would otherwise be safe.
whyNot: Maternal insulin does not cross the placenta. The insulin that delays surfactant is made by the fetal pancreas.

Before birth the fetus of a hyperglycemic mother is hyperglycemic, not hypoglycemic. Neonatal hypoglycemia appears after the cord is cut, when the high fetal insulin is no longer matched by maternal glucose.
Ketoacids do not break down surfactant lipids. Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine is the main surfactant lipid, but this is not how diabetes affects it.
Correct.

questions.stem: He is treated with intratracheal surfactant and mechanical ventilation. On day 3, he has bounding peripheral pulses, a widened pulse pressure, and a continuous murmur at the left upper sternal border. Which of the following best explains the persistence of the structure causing these findings?
options: Persistent high pulmonary vascular resistance with right-to-left ductal flow
Hypoxemia and high prostaglandin E2 levels keeping the ductus open
Raised left atrial pressure holding the foramen ovale open
Incomplete fusion of the septum primum with the endocardial cushions
approach: Recognize the findings: a continuous murmur with bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure means a patent ductus arteriosus.
Recall what normally closes the ductus after birth: a rise in PaO2 and a fall in prostaglandin E2.
Link his prematurity and hypoxemic lung disease to failure of both signals.
questions.why: In the fetus, low oxygen tension and prostaglandin E2 from the placenta keep the ductus arteriosus open. After birth, the rise in PaO2 and the fall in prostaglandin E2 normally close it. In a preterm infant with respiratory distress syndrome, hypoxemia persists and the immature ductus stays sensitive to prostaglandin, so it remains open. As surfactant improves the lungs and pulmonary resistance falls, blood flows from the aorta into the pulmonary artery throughout the cardiac cycle, giving a continuous murmur and bounding pulses. Other complications of this disease and its treatment are bronchopulmonary dysplasia and retinopathy of prematurity from oxygen therapy.
whyNot: High pulmonary resistance with right-to-left flow causes cyanosis without a continuous murmur. A continuous murmur means aortic pressure exceeds pulmonary pressure throughout the cycle, so flow is left to right.
Correct.
Raised left atrial pressure closes the foramen ovale flap. A small atrial shunt also causes no continuous murmur or bounding pulses.
This describes an ostium primum atrial septal defect, a structural defect present from early development. It causes a systolic flow murmur and fixed split S2, not a continuous murmur.

topics: Complications of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome

case: A 68-year-old man comes to the physician because of an 18-month history of progressive shortness of breath on exertion and a dry cough. He smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 25 years and quit 15 years ago. He worked as an accountant and has no known occupational or environmental exposures. He takes no medications. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows fine end-inspiratory crackles at both lung bases and clubbing of the fingers. Pulmonary function testing shows an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.88 (normal 0.70 or greater), a total lung capacity of 61% of predicted (normal 80 to 120), and a DLCO of 42% of predicted (normal 75 to 125). High-resolution CT shows subpleural, basal reticular opacities with honeycombing. Diagnosis: idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.stem: A surgical lung biopsy shows patchy subpleural fibrosis that alternates with areas of normal lung, scattered fibroblastic foci, and honeycomb change. Which of the following best describes the process that produced these changes?
options: Repeated alveolar epithelial injury with TGF-beta driven fibrosis
Th1 cell granulomatous reaction to repeatedly inhaled organic antigens
Neutrophil elastase destruction of alveolar walls distal to terminal bronchioles
Diffuse capillary endothelial injury with protein-rich exudate and hyaline membranes
approach: Recognize the biopsy pattern: patchy fibrosis of different ages, fibroblastic foci, and honeycombing is usual interstitial pneumonia.
Recall the current model of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: repeated small injuries to alveolar epithelium with abnormal repair.
Name the main fibrogenic signal: TGF-beta activates fibroblasts and drives collagen deposition.
questions.why: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is thought to start with repeated injury to alveolar epithelial cells, with risk raised by smoking, older age, and genetic variants. Instead of normal repair, injured epithelium releases TGF-beta and other factors that recruit and activate fibroblasts. The result is the usual interstitial pneumonia pattern: patchy fibrosis that is worst at the bases and under the pleura, fibroblastic foci at the active edge, and honeycomb cysts where lung architecture is destroyed. Areas of different ages side by side reflect injury that happens again and again over time.
whyNot: Correct.

This describes hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which shows poorly formed granulomas centered on bronchioles and a history of exposure to organic dust. He has no exposures and the biopsy shows no granulomas.
Elastase destruction of alveolar walls produces emphysema, an obstructive disease with increased compliance and a low FEV1/FVC ratio. His ratio is high and his lungs are small.
This is diffuse alveolar damage, the lesion of acute respiratory distress syndrome. It develops over days, involves the lungs uniformly, and does not show patchy fibrosis of different ages.

questions.stem: His oxygen saturation is 94% at rest and falls to 86% after a 3-minute walk. Which of the following best explains the fall in saturation with exercise?
options: Right-to-left shunting of blood through intrapulmonary arteriovenous channels
Alveolar hypoventilation from fatigue of the respiratory muscles
Left shift of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve during exercise
Faster red cell transit through capillaries across a thickened barrier
approach: Use Fick law: diffusion falls when the barrier is thicker and the surface area is smaller, both present in fibrosis.
At rest, red cells spend about 0.75 second in the capillary, enough time to equilibrate even with slow diffusion.
With exercise, cardiac output rises and transit time shortens, so oxygen uptake becomes diffusion-limited.
questions.why: Fick law states that gas transfer is proportional to surface area and the pressure difference, and inversely proportional to barrier thickness. In a healthy lung, oxygen uptake is perfusion-limited because blood equilibrates with alveolar gas within the first third of the capillary. Fibrosis thickens the blood-air barrier and destroys capillary surface area, which is why his DLCO is low. At rest there is still enough time to load oxygen, but exercise speeds blood through the capillaries, so blood leaves before it equilibrates and saturation falls. Carbon monoxide uptake is always diffusion-limited, which is why DLCO measures the diffusing capacity.
whyNot: Intrapulmonary arteriovenous shunts occur in hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and hepatopulmonary syndrome. They are not part of pulmonary fibrosis.
Patients with fibrosis breathe rapidly and usually have a normal or low PaCO2. A 3-minute walk does not fatigue the respiratory muscles enough to cause hypoventilation.
Exercise raises temperature, CO2, and acid in working muscle, which shift the curve to the right. A left shift would not cause desaturation in the lung.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following changes in the mechanical properties and connective tissue of his lungs best accounts for his small lung volumes?
options: Increased compliance from destruction of elastic fibers
Decreased compliance from excess interstitial collagen
Increased compliance from impaired elastin cross-linking
Normal compliance with increased chest wall stiffness
approach: Recognize the restrictive pattern: low total lung capacity with a high FEV1/FVC ratio.
Ask what connective tissue change makes lungs stiffer: collagen replacing normal interstitium.
Link stiffness to low compliance, which limits how far the lungs can be inflated.
questions.why: Lung compliance is the change in volume for a given change in pressure. Elastin, cross-linked by the copper-dependent enzyme lysyl oxidase, gives the lung stretch and recoil. Collagen is much less stretchy. In pulmonary fibrosis, fibroblasts lay down large amounts of collagen in the interstitium, so the lungs become stiff and compliance falls. The respiratory muscles cannot expand stiff lungs as far, so total lung capacity and the other volumes fall. Emphysema does the opposite: elastin is destroyed, compliance rises, and the lungs overinflate.
whyNot: Loss of elastic fibers makes lungs floppy and easy to inflate, with high compliance and high total lung capacity. This is emphysema.
Correct.
Poor elastin cross-linking, as with copper deficiency reducing lysyl oxidase activity, weakens elastic recoil and raises compliance. His lungs are stiff, with low compliance.
A stiff chest wall, as in kyphoscoliosis, causes extrapulmonary restriction with normal DLCO. His low DLCO, crackles, and CT findings place the problem in the lung itself.

topics: Elastin versus collagen in the lung

questions.stem: In the same clinic, a 50-year-old woman who has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years has gradually progressive dyspnea. A lung biopsy shows alveoli uniformly filled with pigmented macrophages, mild uniform thickening of the alveolar septa, and no fibroblastic foci or honeycombing. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Fibrotic nonspecific interstitial pneumonia
Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia
Desquamative interstitial pneumonia
Usual interstitial pneumonia
approach: Note the key clues: a heavy smoker and airspaces uniformly filled with pigmented macrophages.
Contrast the patterns: macrophages in airspaces, uniform septal fibrosis, fibroblast plugs, or patchy fibrosis with honeycombing.
Match macrophage-filled alveoli in a smoker to desquamative interstitial pneumonia.
questions.why: Desquamative interstitial pneumonia is a smoking-related interstitial lung disease. The name comes from an old belief that the cells in the alveoli were shed epithelial cells; they are actually macrophages, often containing brown smoker's pigment. The change is uniform throughout the biopsy, with only mild septal thickening. It usually improves with stopping smoking, and its prognosis is much better than that of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
whyNot: Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia shows uniform interstitial inflammation and fibrosis of the same age. Its defining change is in the septa, not macrophages packing the airspaces.
Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia shows polypoid plugs of loose fibroblastic tissue (Masson bodies) in alveolar ducts and alveoli. Macrophages do not dominate the picture.
Correct.
Usual interstitial pneumonia, the pattern of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, is patchy, with fibroblastic foci and honeycombing. Her biopsy has none of these.

dx: Chronic simple silicosis in a sandblaster
case: A 57-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-year history of slowly worsening shortness of breath on exertion and a dry cough. He has worked as a sandblaster in a shipyard for 26 years and often did not wear respiratory protection. He has never smoked. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 82/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. Lung examination shows a few scattered inspiratory crackles in the upper lung fields. A chest x-ray shows many small, rounded nodules concentrated in both upper lobes and thin rims of calcification around enlarged hilar lymph nodes. Diagnosis: chronic simple silicosis.

questions.stem: He has an increased risk of developing pulmonary tuberculosis. Which of the following best explains this risk?
options: Silica-induced loss of secretory IgA in airway secretions
Silica-induced depletion of CD4+ helper T cells in hilar nodes
Replacement of ciliated epithelium in upper lobe bronchi by squamous cells
Impaired mycobacterial killing by silica-damaged macrophages
approach: Identify the cell that eats silica: the alveolar macrophage.
Recall what silica does inside it: it damages the phagolysosome and activates the inflammasome, injuring or killing the cell.
Link this to tuberculosis, which is controlled mainly by macrophages that must kill the bacilli they ingest.
questions.why: Inhaled silica particles are taken up by alveolar macrophages. Inside the phagolysosome, crystalline silica damages the membrane, releases enzymes, activates the inflammasome, and can kill the cell. The injured macrophages release cytokines and growth factors that drive the fibrotic nodules. These same macrophages are the main defense against Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and silica-damaged macrophages kill mycobacteria poorly. Silicosis therefore raises the risk of active tuberculosis. Other pneumoconiosis features to recall: coal dust also affects the upper lobes, asbestosis affects the lower lobes with ferruginous bodies, and berylliosis causes noncaseating granulomas.
whyNot: Silica does not reduce secretory IgA. IgA deficiency causes recurrent sinus and lung infections with ordinary bacteria, not tuberculosis.
Systemic CD4+ T cell loss, as in HIV infection, raises tuberculosis risk, but silica does not deplete CD4+ T cells.
Squamous metaplasia from smoking impairs mucus clearance and favors bacterial bronchitis. It does not explain the specific link between silica and tuberculosis, and he has never smoked.
Correct.

questions.stem: His 45-year-old cousin works in a cotton textile mill. He has chest tightness, cough, and wheezing that are worst on the first day back at work after a weekend and improve as the work week goes on. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Bagassosis
Byssinosis
Silo-filler disease
Berylliosis
approach: Note the exposure: cotton dust in a textile mill.
Note the timing: symptoms worst on the first workday after time away and easing as the week goes on.
Match cotton dust with this weekly pattern to byssinosis.
questions.why: Byssinosis is an occupational airway disease caused by dust from cotton, flax, or hemp. Contaminants in the dust, including bacterial endotoxin, trigger bronchoconstriction and airway inflammation. The classic feature is chest tightness and wheezing on the first day back at work after a break, which lessens with continued exposure over the week. Years of exposure can cause chronic airflow obstruction.
whyNot: Bagassosis is hypersensitivity pneumonitis from moldy sugarcane fiber (bagasse). It causes fever, cough, and interstitial disease after exposure, without the weekly pattern.
Correct.
Silo-filler disease follows inhalation of nitrogen dioxide in a freshly filled silo. It causes acute bronchiolitis and pulmonary edema, sometimes with later bronchiolitis obliterans.
Berylliosis follows exposure to beryllium in aerospace, electronics, or nuclear work. It causes noncaseating granulomas similar to sarcoidosis.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old dairy farmer who lives nearby develops fever, chills, cough, and dyspnea 6 hours after forking moldy hay. The symptoms resolve over 2 days and recur with each new exposure. A lung biopsy shows lymphocytic infiltrates centered on the bronchioles and poorly formed noncaseating interstitial granulomas. Which of the following immune mechanisms best explains his illness?
options: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation within minutes of exposure
Th2 cytokine-driven eosinophilic inflammation of bronchial walls
Immune complex and T cell reactions to inhaled antigens
Autoantibodies against type IV collagen in alveolar basement membranes
approach: Note the trigger: an organic dust (moldy hay with thermophilic actinomycetes).
Note the timing and pathology: fever hours after exposure, lymphocytes around bronchioles, and poorly formed granulomas.
Match this to hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which combines type III (immune complex) and type IV (T cell) reactions.
questions.why: This is farmer lung, a form of hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by spores of thermophilic actinomycetes in moldy hay. In the acute form, antibodies against the inhaled antigen form immune complexes in the alveolar walls (type III), which explains the onset 4 to 8 hours after exposure with fever and chills. With repeated exposure, T cell-mediated inflammation (type IV) produces lymphocytic infiltrates and poorly formed granulomas. Asthma differs in being a type I, IgE-mediated airway disease that begins within minutes and has eosinophils and no interstitial granulomas.
whyNot: This is a type I reaction, as in allergic asthma. It begins within minutes and causes wheezing, not fever, interstitial granulomas, and onset hours after exposure.
Th2 cytokines and eosinophils drive allergic asthma. The biopsy here shows lymphocytes and granulomas in the interstitium, not eosinophilic bronchial inflammation.
Correct.
Antibodies against type IV collagen cause Goodpasture syndrome, a type II reaction with lung hemorrhage and glomerulonephritis. Inhaled antigens are not involved.

topics: Hypersensitivity reaction types in the lung

questions.stem: Spirometry in the sandblaster shows an FEV1 of 62% of predicted (normal 80 or greater), an FVC of 60% of predicted (normal 80 or greater), and an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.84 (normal 0.70 or greater). Total lung capacity by body plethysmography is 64% of predicted (normal 80 to 120). Which of the following flow-volume loop patterns is most likely?
options: Narrow loop at low lung volumes with a normal expiratory shape
Concave, scooped-out expiratory limb beginning at high lung volumes
Flat plateaus on both the inspiratory and the expiratory limbs
Flat plateau on the inspiratory limb with a normal expiratory limb
approach: Read the numbers: FEV1 and FVC are both reduced, the ratio is normal, and total lung capacity is low.
Classify the pattern as restrictive.
Predict the loop: a small loop shifted toward low lung volumes, with a normal-shaped expiratory limb.
questions.why: In restrictive disease, stiff lungs hold less air, so total lung capacity and FVC fall. FEV1 falls about in proportion, and the extra elastic recoil keeps airways open, so the FEV1/FVC ratio is normal or high. On a flow-volume loop, the whole loop is narrow and sits at lower lung volumes, but the expiratory limb keeps its normal shape. In obstructive disease, the expiratory limb is scooped out and the loop shifts to high lung volumes. Upper airway lesions flatten one or both limbs into plateaus.
whyNot: Correct.
A scooped-out expiratory limb at high lung volumes is the obstructive pattern of asthma or COPD. His FEV1/FVC ratio is normal and his total lung capacity is low.
Flattening of both limbs is the pattern of a fixed upper airway obstruction, such as tracheal stenosis. It limits peak flows without lowering total lung capacity.
Flattening of only the inspiratory limb points to a variable obstruction outside the thorax, such as vocal cord paralysis. Lung volumes are normal.

dx: Pulmonary sarcoidosis with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and hypercalcemia
case: A 36-year-old Black woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of dry cough, shortness of breath on exertion, fatigue, and increased thirst and urination. Temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), pulse is 86/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. Lung examination shows a few scattered crackles. Serum studies show a calcium concentration of 11.6 mg/dL (normal 8.5 to 10.2), a parathyroid hormone concentration of 8 pg/mL (normal 10 to 65), and an angiotensin-converting enzyme activity of 98 U/L (normal 8 to 52). A chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with reticular opacities in both lungs. Transbronchial biopsy shows noncaseating granulomas, and stains for acid-fast bacilli and fungi are negative. Diagnosis: pulmonary sarcoidosis.

questions.stem: Her serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D concentration is increased. Which of the following best explains her hypercalcemia?
options: Parathyroid hormone-related peptide secreted by granuloma cells
Unregulated 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity in granuloma macrophages
Increased renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity driven by parathyroid hormone
Increased hepatic 25-hydroxylation of dietary vitamin D
approach: Note the pattern: high calcium, low parathyroid hormone, and high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.
Low parathyroid hormone means the kidney is not the source of the extra active vitamin D.
Identify the source outside the kidney: activated macrophages in granulomas express 1-alpha-hydroxylase that escapes normal feedback.
questions.why: Active vitamin D (calcitriol, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) is made by adding a hydroxyl group at carbon 1 of 25-hydroxyvitamin D. In the kidney, this step is driven by parathyroid hormone and shut off when calcium is high. Macrophages activated by IFN-gamma in sarcoid granulomas also express 1-alpha-hydroxylase, and this enzyme is not controlled by parathyroid hormone or calcium. Excess calcitriol increases intestinal calcium absorption, causing hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria, which suppress parathyroid hormone. High urine calcium explains her thirst and frequent urination.
whyNot: Parathyroid hormone-related peptide causes hypercalcemia in squamous cell carcinoma and some other cancers. It usually leaves 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D low or normal, and granulomas do not make it.
Correct.
Her parathyroid hormone is low, as expected when calcium is high. The kidney enzyme is turned down, not up.
Liver 25-hydroxylation is not tightly regulated and is not the step that sets active vitamin D levels. It would not explain a high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D with a low parathyroid hormone.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the immune process that forms and maintains her granulomas?
options: Th2 cells releasing IL-4 that drives IgE class switching
Th17 cells releasing IL-17 that recruits neutrophils
Th1 cells releasing IFN-gamma to activate macrophages
Regulatory T cells releasing IL-10 that deactivates macrophages
approach: Recognize the lesion: a noncaseating granuloma made of epithelioid macrophages, giant cells, and surrounding lymphocytes.
Recall that granulomas are a Th1 response.
Link IFN-gamma from Th1 cells to macrophage activation, and TNF-alpha from macrophages to keeping the granuloma intact.
questions.why: In sarcoidosis, an unknown antigen is presented to CD4+ T cells, which take on a Th1 profile. Macrophages release IL-12, which drives Th1 differentiation, and Th1 cells release IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages and turns them into epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells. Activated macrophages release TNF-alpha, which recruits cells and holds the granuloma together. The same pathway contains tuberculosis, which is why blocking TNF-alpha can reactivate latent tuberculosis.
whyNot: IL-4 from Th2 cells drives IgE production and allergic inflammation, as in asthma. It does not build epithelioid granulomas.
IL-17 recruits neutrophils and helps fight extracellular bacteria and fungi. Neutrophils are not the main cells of a sarcoid granuloma.
Correct.
IL-10 suppresses macrophages and limits inflammation. Granulomas form when macrophages are activated, not deactivated.

questions.stem: Endobronchial ultrasound-guided needle aspiration is planned for an enlarged lymph node at her left hilum. The node lies against the most superior structure in the root of the left lung. Which of the following structures is this most likely to be?
options: Left pulmonary artery
Left main bronchus
Left superior pulmonary vein
Left inferior pulmonary vein
approach: Picture the root of the left lung from the medial side.
Recall the rule: on the left the pulmonary artery is the highest structure; on the right it lies in front of the bronchus, with the upper lobe bronchus above it.
The veins are anterior and inferior at both hila.
questions.why: Each lung root contains a pulmonary artery, a main bronchus, two pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, nerves, and lymph nodes. On the left, the pulmonary artery arches over the main bronchus and is the most superior structure. On the right, the upper lobe (eparterial) bronchus branches off above the artery, and the right pulmonary artery lies in front of the bronchus. On both sides the pulmonary veins are the most anterior and inferior structures. Enlarged hilar nodes in sarcoidosis sit among these structures.
whyNot: Correct.
At the left hilum the main bronchus lies below the pulmonary artery and toward the back. At the right hilum, the upper lobe bronchus is the highest structure.
The superior pulmonary vein lies anterior and inferior to the pulmonary artery at each hilum.
The inferior pulmonary vein is the lowest structure in the lung root, close to the pulmonary ligament.

questions.stem: Pulmonary function testing shows a total lung capacity of 68% of predicted (normal 80 to 120) and a DLCO of 52% of predicted (normal 75 to 125). A 60-year-old man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has a similar total lung capacity because of respiratory muscle weakness, and his PaCO2 is 52 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45). Which of the following findings is most likely in the man?
options: Reduced DLCO and widened A-a gradient
Normal DLCO and widened A-a gradient
Increased DLCO and widened A-a gradient
Normal DLCO and normal A-a gradient
approach: Classify each restriction: hers is in the lung tissue; his comes from weak respiratory muscles.
In muscle weakness the alveolar walls and capillaries are normal, so diffusion is normal.
His low oxygen comes from hypoventilation alone, which lowers PAO2 and PaO2 together and keeps the A-a gradient normal.
questions.why: Restriction can arise inside the lung or outside it. Intrinsic disease, such as sarcoidosis or fibrosis, damages the alveolar walls, so DLCO falls and ventilation-perfusion mismatch widens the A-a gradient. Extrapulmonary restriction comes from weak muscles, a deformed chest wall, or obesity. The lung tissue is healthy, so DLCO adjusted for lung volume is normal. If ventilation falls, PaCO2 rises and alveolar PO2 falls, but arterial PO2 falls by the same amount, so the A-a gradient stays normal.
whyNot: This is her pattern. Granulomas and fibrosis thicken the blood-air barrier and disturb ventilation-perfusion matching, so DLCO falls and the A-a gradient widens.
A widened A-a gradient means a problem in gas exchange inside the lung. His lungs are normal, so his gradient stays normal.
DLCO rises with polycythemia or alveolar hemorrhage, which add hemoglobin to bind CO. Neither applies, and his gas exchange surface is normal.
Correct.

dx: Allergic asthma with an acute exacerbation
case: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of 6 hours of increasing shortness of breath, wheezing, and cough that began while visiting a friend who has two cats. She has a history of allergic rhinitis and atopic dermatitis. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg, with a pulsus paradoxus of 18 mm Hg (normal less than 10). She speaks in short phrases and uses her neck muscles to breathe. Lung examination shows diffuse expiratory wheezes with a prolonged expiratory phase. Peak expiratory flow is 40% of her personal best. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 91%. Diagnosis: acute exacerbation of allergic asthma.

questions.stem: Microscopy of her sputum shows spiral-shaped mucus casts and colorless, bipyramidal crystals. Which of the following findings would most likely be seen on a biopsy of her bronchial wall?
options: Thickened subepithelial basement membrane and goblet cell hyperplasia
Destruction of alveolar walls distal to the terminal bronchioles
Permanent bronchial dilation with necrotizing transmural inflammation
Noncaseating granulomas in the bronchial submucosa
approach: Identify the sputum findings: Curschmann spirals (shed epithelium in mucus casts) and Charcot-Leyden crystals (from eosinophil protein).
These point to eosinophilic airway inflammation of asthma.
Recall the airway remodeling of asthma: thickened basement membrane, goblet cell hyperplasia, submucosal gland enlargement, and smooth muscle hypertrophy.
questions.why: Allergic asthma is a chronic Th2 inflammatory disease of the bronchi and bronchioles. Charcot-Leyden crystals form from galectin-10 released by eosinophils, and Curschmann spirals are mucus casts of small airways with shed epithelial cells. Over time the airway wall remodels: collagen is laid down beneath the epithelium so the basement membrane looks thick, goblet cells and submucosal glands increase, and smooth muscle hypertrophies. Asthma can also be triggered by nonallergic factors such as viral infections, cold air, exercise, and aspirin.
whyNot: Correct.
Alveolar wall destruction is emphysema. It affects the airspaces beyond the bronchioles, not the bronchial wall.
Necrotizing inflammation that destroys the wall and leaves the bronchus permanently dilated is bronchiectasis. Asthma airways are narrowed, and the obstruction is reversible.
Noncaseating granulomas suggest sarcoidosis or berylliosis. They are not a feature of asthma.

questions.stem: On arrival, arterial blood gas analysis on room air showed a pH of 7.48 (normal 7.35 to 7.45) and a PaCO2 of 31 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45). After 3 hours of treatment, she is drowsy, and breath sounds are faint with little wheezing. Repeat analysis shows a pH of 7.36, a PaCO2 of 45 mm Hg, and a PaO2 of 60 mm Hg (normal 75 to 100). Which of the following best explains the change in her blood gas values?
options: Resolution of bronchospasm with a return to normal ventilation
Reduced ventilatory drive after correction of hypoxemia
Respiratory muscle fatigue with falling alveolar ventilation
Development of metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
approach: In acute asthma, hypoxemia and airway receptors drive hyperventilation, so PaCO2 starts low.
A PaCO2 that climbs back to normal while she is still hypoxemic means ventilation is failing.
Drowsiness and a quiet chest confirm tiring muscles and little air movement.
questions.why: Early in an asthma attack, patients breathe fast and blow off CO2, producing respiratory alkalosis. Air trapping forces the respiratory muscles to work at a mechanical disadvantage, and they eventually tire. As alveolar ventilation falls, PaCO2 rises toward normal and then above it. A normal PaCO2 in a patient who is still working hard to breathe is therefore an ominous sign of impending respiratory failure. A quiet chest means little air is moving, not that the obstruction has resolved.
whyNot: Improving asthma brings better air movement, louder breath sounds, a clearer mind, and higher PaO2. Her drowsiness, faint breath sounds, and low PaO2 show the opposite.
Loss of hypoxic drive with oxygen therapy is a concern in some patients with chronic CO2 retention. She has no chronic lung disease, and her PaO2 is still low.
Correct.
Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis lowers PaCO2. Her PaCO2 rose.

questions.stem: Her symptoms improve, then return 6 hours later without further exposure, and her sputum now contains many eosinophils. Which of the following cytokines most directly drives the production and activation of the cells that dominate this second phase?
options: Interleukin-4 from Th2 cells
Interleukin-5 from Th2 cells
Interferon-gamma from Th1 cells
Interleukin-13 from Th2 cells
approach: Recognize the late phase response: symptoms return 4 to 8 hours after exposure, driven by recruited inflammatory cells.
Identify the dominant cell: eosinophils.
Match eosinophil production and activation to IL-5 from Th2 cells.
questions.why: Allergic asthma is a type I hypersensitivity reaction. In the early phase, within minutes, allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells, which release histamine, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins, causing bronchospasm. In the late phase, 4 to 8 hours later, recruited cells sustain the inflammation. Th2 cells release IL-4 (IgE class switching), IL-5 (eosinophil production in the marrow, recruitment, and activation), and IL-13 (mucus secretion and airway hyperresponsiveness). Eosinophils release major basic protein and other granule contents that injure the airway epithelium.
whyNot: IL-4 drives B cell class switching to IgE and Th2 differentiation. It sets up the allergy but does not directly produce and activate eosinophils.
Correct.
IFN-gamma activates macrophages in Th1 responses and tends to suppress Th2 inflammation.
IL-13 drives mucus production by goblet cells and airway hyperresponsiveness. It is not the main growth and activation factor for eosinophils.

topics: Early and late phase allergic responses

questions.stem: During the attack, smooth muscle contraction reduces the radius of her medium-sized bronchi by half. Assuming laminar flow and no other changes, the resistance of these airways increases by approximately which of the following factors?
options: 4-fold
8-fold
16-fold
32-fold
approach: Recall Poiseuille law: resistance equals 8 times viscosity times length, divided by pi times radius to the fourth power.
Halving the radius divides the denominator by 2 to the fourth power, which is 16.
Resistance rises 16-fold, so the same flow needs 16 times the pressure difference.
questions.why: Poiseuille law shows that airway resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of the radius. Halving the radius raises resistance 16-fold, which is why modest bronchoconstriction causes severe obstruction. Lung volume also matters: at low lung volumes, airways lose radial traction and narrow, so resistance rises. During forced expiration, rising pleural pressure also compresses the airways, which is why wheezing is loudest in expiration. Gas density affects resistance where flow is turbulent, so breathing a low-density helium-oxygen mixture can lower resistance in large airways.
whyNot: A 4-fold rise would follow if resistance depended on the square of the radius, as cross-sectional area does. Resistance depends on the fourth power.
An 8-fold rise would follow from a cube relation. Resistance depends on the fourth power of the radius.
Correct.
A 32-fold rise would follow from a fifth-power relation. Resistance depends on the fourth power of the radius.

dx: Bronchiectasis from primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome)
case: A 26-year-old man comes to the physician because of a daily cough productive of large amounts of purulent sputum. He has had recurrent sinus infections and pneumonias since early childhood. He and his wife have been unable to conceive for 2 years. He has never smoked. Temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 120/74 mm Hg. Heart sounds are loudest to the right of the sternum. There is clubbing of the fingers, and coarse crackles are heard over both lower lung fields. CT shows dextrocardia, a left-sided liver, and dilated, thick-walled bronchi in both lower lobes. Semen analysis shows a normal sperm count with no motile sperm. Diagnosis: bronchiectasis due to primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome).

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the reversed position of his heart and liver?
options: Failed neural crest migration into the conotruncal septum
Abnormal fusion of the superior and inferior endocardial cushions
Absent nodal ciliary flow at left-right patterning
Displacement of the heart by a hypoplastic right lung
approach: Note that both the heart and the liver are reversed: this is situs inversus.
Recall that motile cilia at the embryonic node beat to create a leftward fluid flow that sets the left-right axis.
With immotile cilia, sidedness is decided by chance, so about half of patients have situs inversus.
questions.why: Primary ciliary dyskinesia is usually autosomal recessive and most often affects the dynein arms of the ciliary axoneme. In the early embryo, rotating cilia at the primitive node push fluid to the left, which turns on left-sided genes and sets left-right patterning. When these cilia cannot move, organ sidedness becomes random, so about half of patients have situs inversus. Kartagener syndrome is the combination of situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis. Men are usually infertile because sperm flagella share the same axoneme structure and cannot swim.
whyNot: Neural crest failure in the outflow tract causes defects such as tetralogy of Fallot and truncus arteriosus. It does not reverse the position of the organs.
Endocardial cushion defects cause atrioventricular septal defects, often in Down syndrome. They do not change the left-right position of organs.
Correct.
A small right lung can pull the heart to the right (dextroposition), but it would not move the liver to the left. His organs are mirror-imaged.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains his recurrent airway infections?
options: Abnormal CFTR chloride transport causing dehydrated mucus
Failed dynein-driven sliding of microtubule doublets
Squamous metaplasia replacing the ciliated epithelium
Hyperplasia of submucosal glands with excess mucus
approach: Link the three clues: recurrent sinus and lung infections, immotile sperm, and situs inversus all depend on motile cilia or flagella.
Recall the axoneme: 9 outer microtubule doublets around a central pair, with dynein arms that make the doublets slide.
Without dynein, cilia cannot beat, so the mucociliary escalator stops and mucus and bacteria stay in the airways.
questions.why: Airway cilia have a 9 plus 2 axoneme: nine outer doublets around two central microtubules. Dynein arms on each doublet use ATP to walk along the neighboring doublet, and this sliding bends the cilium. Coordinated beating moves the mucus layer up toward the pharynx at a few millimeters per minute, carrying trapped particles and bacteria out of the lung. When dynein is defective, mucus pools in the sinuses and bronchi, and repeated infection follows. Smoking causes a similar but acquired failure by paralyzing cilia and replacing ciliated cells with squamous epithelium.
whyNot: Cystic fibrosis causes thick mucus and bronchiectasis, but the cilia and sperm tails are normal. Infertility in men with cystic fibrosis comes from absent vasa deferentia, which leaves no sperm in the semen. His sperm count is normal.
Correct.
Squamous metaplasia is a response to cigarette smoke and other irritants. He has never smoked, and metaplasia would not explain motionless sperm.
Mucous gland hyperplasia is the lesion of chronic bronchitis in smokers. It would not explain infertility with immotile sperm or situs inversus.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the permanent dilation of his bronchi?
options: Loss of radial traction after destruction of alveolar walls
Smooth muscle hypertrophy with episodic bronchospasm
Traction on airways from surrounding interstitial fibrosis
Necrotizing infection destroying muscle and elastic tissue
approach: Bronchiectasis needs two things: obstruction that keeps secretions in the airway and infection that damages the wall.
Here, failed mucociliary clearance provides the retained secretions.
Repeated necrotizing infection destroys the muscle and elastic tissue of the wall, so the bronchus stays widened.
questions.why: Bronchiectasis is permanent dilation of bronchi and bronchioles. It develops when secretions are retained and infected again and again. Neutrophils and bacterial enzymes destroy smooth muscle, elastic tissue, and cartilage, and the weakened wall dilates. Causes include cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, and blockage by a tumor or foreign body. Patients have large amounts of foul, purulent sputum, hemoptysis from enlarged bronchial arteries, clubbing, and, after years of chronic inflammation, risk of secondary (AA) amyloidosis.
whyNot: Loss of alveolar attachments lets small airways collapse during expiration in emphysema. It does not permanently widen the bronchi.
Smooth muscle hypertrophy and spasm narrow the airways in asthma, and the narrowing is reversible.
Traction bronchiectasis occurs in advanced pulmonary fibrosis, where contracting scar pulls airways open. He has no interstitial fibrosis, and his disease is driven by infection.
Correct.

questions.stem: A resected segment of his lower lobe shows several dilated airways. The pathologist confirms that these airways are bronchi and not bronchioles. Which of the following wall features is the most reliable basis for this conclusion?
options: Cartilage plates with submucosal glands
Spiral smooth muscle beneath the mucosa
Ciliated columnar cells lining the lumen
Club cells scattered among ciliated cells
approach: Recall the features that stop at the bronchus-bronchiole transition: cartilage plates and submucosal glands.
Note which features continue into bronchioles: smooth muscle and, in the larger ones, ciliated cells.
Choose the feature found only in bronchi.
questions.why: Bronchi have plates of hyaline cartilage, submucosal seromucous glands, and many goblet cells. Bronchioles, about 1 mm across or smaller, have no cartilage and no glands, and their goblet cells thin out and are replaced by club cells near the terminal bronchioles. Because bronchioles lack cartilage, they stay open only through smooth muscle tone and the radial pull of attached alveolar walls. That is why they collapse in emphysema, when the alveolar attachments are destroyed.
whyNot: Correct.
Smooth muscle lines both bronchi and bronchioles. In bronchioles it makes up a larger share of the wall, so its presence does not separate the two.
Larger bronchioles are also lined by ciliated columnar cells, and the lining changes only gradually along the airway, so this cannot separate them.
Club cells are typical of bronchioles, especially terminal bronchioles. Their presence would point toward a bronchiole.

case: A 63-year-old woman comes to the physician because of increasing shortness of breath and swelling of her ankles for 2 months. She has smoked 1.5 packs of cigarettes daily for 40 years. For the past 5 years, she has had a cough productive of mucoid sputum on most days for at least 3 months each year. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg. She is overweight and has central cyanosis. Examination shows scattered rhonchi and wheezes, jugular venous distention, a left parasternal heave, a loud pulmonic component of S2, an enlarged liver, and pitting edema of both ankles. Hemoglobin concentration is 17.8 g/dL (normal 12 to 16). Spirometry shows an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.55 (normal 0.70 or greater). Diagnosis: chronic bronchitis with cor pulmonale.

questions.stem: Which of the following changes in her bronchial walls best explains her chronic productive cough?
options: Thickened basement membrane with many eosinophils
Submucosal gland layer over half the bronchial wall thickness
Permanent bronchial dilation with destruction of the cartilage
Enlarged airspaces with alveolar wall destruction
approach: Recognize chronic bronchitis by its clinical definition: productive cough for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years.
Ask what makes the extra mucus: enlarged submucosal mucous glands.
Recall how this is measured: the Reid index, gland thickness divided by wall thickness, is above 0.5.
questions.why: Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically by a productive cough for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years. Smoke and other irritants cause hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the submucosal mucous glands of the large airways and more goblet cells in smaller airways. The Reid index compares the thickness of the gland layer with the thickness of the wall between epithelium and cartilage. It is normally under 0.4 and is above 0.5 in chronic bronchitis. Mucus plugging and inflammation of small airways cause the airflow obstruction.
whyNot: A thick basement membrane with eosinophils is the remodeling of asthma, which causes episodic wheezing more than daily sputum.
Correct.
Destruction of the wall with permanent dilation is bronchiectasis. It produces large volumes of purulent sputum, often with hemoptysis and clubbing.
Alveolar wall destruction is emphysema, which affects the airspaces and causes dyspnea with little sputum.

questions.stem: During a later exacerbation she needs noninvasive ventilation for hypercapnia, and enteral feeding is started. Her physician chooses a formula that supplies a larger share of calories as fat than as carbohydrate. Which of the following best explains this choice?
options: Fat oxidation releases less CO2 for each liter of O2 consumed
Fat oxidation uses less O2 for each kilocalorie produced
Fat oxidation increases red cell 2,3-BPG and oxygen unloading
Carbohydrate oxidation lowers the respiratory quotient toward 0.7
approach: Define the respiratory quotient: CO2 produced divided by O2 consumed.
Recall typical values: carbohydrate 1.0, protein about 0.8, fat about 0.7.
Apply it: less CO2 per unit of O2 means less CO2 that her weak ventilation must remove.
questions.why: The respiratory quotient (RQ) is the ratio of CO2 produced to O2 consumed. For glucose, C6H12O6 plus 6 O2 gives 6 CO2, so RQ is 1.0. Fats are more reduced molecules that need more O2 for each carbon, so RQ is about 0.7, and protein is about 0.8. A patient with hypercapnic lung disease cannot easily raise ventilation. A carbohydrate-heavy diet, and especially overfeeding, raises CO2 production and the ventilation needed to clear it. Shifting calories toward fat lowers CO2 production and ventilatory demand.
whyNot: Correct.
Fat actually uses slightly more O2 per kilocalorie than carbohydrate. The advantage of fat is the lower CO2 output.
2,3-BPG is made from a glycolytic intermediate in red cells. Burning fat does not raise it.
Carbohydrate oxidation has a respiratory quotient of 1.0, the highest of the three fuels. A value near 0.7 reflects fat.

questions.stem: Echocardiography shows a dilated, hypertrophied right ventricle and an estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 55 mm Hg (normal less than 35). Which of the following best describes the main cause of her pulmonary hypertension and its vascular change?
options: BMPR2 mutation causing plexiform lesions in small arteries
Raised left atrial pressure transmitted back to pulmonary veins
Hypoxic vasoconstriction with medial hypertrophy of arterioles
Organized thromboemboli obstructing the pulmonary arteries
approach: Place her in a pulmonary hypertension group: she has lung disease with chronic hypoxemia.
Recall the reflex: low alveolar oxygen constricts the pulmonary arterioles that supply it.
Chronic constriction causes muscle thickening in small arteries, raising pressure and overloading the right ventricle (cor pulmonale).
questions.why: Pulmonary hypertension is grouped by cause: pulmonary arterial hypertension (including BMPR2 mutations), left heart disease, lung disease or hypoxia, chronic thromboembolism, and other causes. In chronic bronchitis, poorly ventilated alveoli cause widespread hypoxic vasoconstriction. Over time, smooth muscle in small arteries and arterioles hypertrophies, the intima thickens, and resistance stays high. The right ventricle hypertrophies and then fails, which is cor pulmonale. Her raised hemoglobin, from erythropoietin released in response to hypoxemia, adds blood viscosity and makes it worse.
whyNot: BMPR2 mutations cause heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension, with plexiform lesions in small arteries. This is a disease of the vessels themselves, not of airway disease.
Pulmonary hypertension from left heart disease follows left ventricular failure or mitral valve disease. Her findings point to the right heart and lungs.
Correct.
Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension follows repeated or unresolved emboli. Nothing in her history suggests emboli.

questions.stem: Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows a pH of 7.34 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), a PaCO2 of 60 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45), and a bicarbonate concentration of 31 mEq/L (normal 22 to 28). Which of the following best describes her acid-base status?
options: Acute respiratory acidosis without renal compensation
Chronic respiratory acidosis plus a superimposed metabolic acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis with compensatory hypoventilation
Chronic respiratory acidosis with expected renal compensation
approach: The pH is low and PaCO2 is high, so the primary problem is respiratory acidosis.
Estimate chronic compensation: bicarbonate rises about 3 to 4 mEq/L for each 10 mm Hg rise in PaCO2. A 20 mm Hg rise predicts about 24 + 7 = 31 mEq/L.
Her bicarbonate matches, so there is no second disorder.
questions.why: In respiratory acidosis the kidneys compensate by making and retaining more bicarbonate. This takes 3 to 5 days. Acutely, bicarbonate rises only about 1 mEq/L for each 10 mm Hg rise in PaCO2, mostly from buffering. Chronically it rises about 3 to 4 mEq/L for each 10 mm Hg. Her PaCO2 is 20 mm Hg above normal, so a bicarbonate near 31 mEq/L is the expected chronic response, and her pH is close to normal. If the bicarbonate were well above or below the expected value, a mixed disorder would be present.
whyNot: Acutely, bicarbonate rises only about 1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in PaCO2, so it would be about 26 mEq/L, and the pH would be much lower, near 7.26.
An added metabolic acidosis would hold bicarbonate below the expected value. Her bicarbonate matches the expected chronic rise.
A primary metabolic alkalosis would give an alkaline pH. Her pH is acidic, so the primary problem is respiratory acidosis.
Correct.

dx: Panacinar emphysema from alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ)
case: A 41-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-year history of progressive shortness of breath on exertion. He has never smoked. Temperature is 36.7 °C (98.1 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. He is thin, with an increased anteroposterior chest diameter. He breathes out through pursed lips. The chest is hyperresonant, and breath sounds are decreased with a prolonged expiratory phase. A chest x-ray shows hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms and increased lucency at both bases. Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin concentration is 18 mg/dL (normal 100 to 200), and genotyping shows the PiZZ genotype. Serum alanine aminotransferase activity is 64 U/L (normal 7 to 40). Diagnosis: panacinar emphysema due to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

questions.stem: A liver biopsy shows round, PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules in periportal hepatocytes. Which of the following best explains both his liver disease and his lung disease?
options: Absent gene transcription with no protein made in any tissue
Excess protein secretion that overwhelms hepatic clearance
Normal secretion of a protein unable to bind neutrophil elastase
Retention of misfolded protein in the hepatocyte ER
approach: Link the globules to their content: misfolded Z protein polymerized in the endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes.
Trapped protein injures the liver (gain of toxic function).
Too little protein reaches the blood and lung, so neutrophil elastase acts unopposed (loss of function).
questions.why: Alpha-1 antitrypsin is made in hepatocytes and encoded by SERPINA1. Its alleles are codominant: each allele contributes to the plasma level, so PiMM is normal, PiMZ is intermediate, and PiZZ is about 10 to 15% of normal. The Z mutation (Glu342Lys) makes the protein misfold and polymerize in the endoplasmic reticulum, where it forms PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules that can cause hepatitis and cirrhosis. Because little protein is secreted, the lungs lack their main inhibitor of neutrophil elastase, and panacinar emphysema develops early, especially in smokers.
whyNot: Null alleles that make no protein cause severe emphysema, but there is nothing to collect in the liver, so the liver is spared.
His plasma level is low, not high. The protein is trapped inside hepatocytes and not secreted.
A secreted but nonfunctional protein could cause emphysema, but it would not build up as globules in hepatocytes.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following patterns of airspace enlargement within the acinus is most likely present in his lungs?
options: Enlarged respiratory bronchioles with sparing of distal alveoli
Enlarged distal acini along pleura and septa forming bullae
Uniform enlargement from respiratory bronchioles to alveoli
Irregular enlargement of airspaces adjacent to old scars
approach: Link the cause to the pattern: a body-wide lack of antiprotease affects the whole acinus evenly.
Recall the three patterns: centriacinar (central, upper lobes, smoking), panacinar (whole acinus, lower lobes, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency), and paraseptal (edges of the acinus near pleura).
Match his basal lucency to panacinar emphysema.
questions.why: Emphysema is permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole with destruction of their walls. In smokers, damage starts where smoke particles land and inflammatory cells gather, in the respiratory bronchioles of the upper lobes, giving centriacinar emphysema. In alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, the antiprotease shield is low everywhere, so the entire acinus is destroyed evenly. It is usually most severe in the lower lobes. Air trapping produces the barrel chest, and pursed-lip breathing keeps airway pressure up to delay collapse during expiration.
whyNot: Centriacinar emphysema enlarges the central respiratory bronchioles and spares the distal alveoli. It is the smoking pattern and is worst in the upper lobes.
Paraseptal emphysema affects the distal acinus next to the pleura and septa. Its subpleural bullae can rupture and cause spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults.
Correct.
Irregular emphysema occurs next to areas of scarring, such as healed infections. It is usually patchy and does not explain diffuse disease at both bases.

questions.stem: His FEV1/FVC ratio is 0.48 (normal 0.70 or greater). Which of the following sets of additional findings is most likely?
options: Raised TLC, low DLCO, normal PaCO2
Raised TLC, normal DLCO, raised PaCO2
Reduced TLC, low DLCO, normal PaCO2
Reduced TLC, normal DLCO, raised PaCO2
approach: The low FEV1/FVC ratio confirms obstruction; loss of elastic recoil and air trapping raise total lung capacity and residual volume.
Destroyed alveolar walls and their capillaries reduce the surface for diffusion, so DLCO falls.
Ventilation and perfusion are lost together, and he breathes harder, so blood gases stay near normal until late.
questions.why: COPD is confirmed by an FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7 after a bronchodilator. In emphysema, elastic recoil is lost, so airways collapse in expiration, air is trapped, and total lung capacity and residual volume rise. Loss of alveolar walls and their capillaries lowers DLCO. Because ventilation and blood flow are lost together, ventilation-perfusion matching is fairly well kept, and the patient works hard to breathe, so PaO2 and PaCO2 stay near normal until late (the pink puffer). In chronic bronchitis, DLCO is normal, but poorly ventilated, well-perfused areas cause hypoxemia and hypercapnia early (the blue bloater).
whyNot: Correct.
This is the pattern of predominant chronic bronchitis. The alveolar surface is preserved, so DLCO is normal, but ventilation-perfusion mismatch causes early hypoxemia and hypercapnia.
Low total lung capacity with low DLCO is the pattern of intrinsic restrictive disease, such as fibrosis. His low FEV1/FVC ratio and hyperinflation show obstruction.
Low total lung capacity with normal DLCO and hypercapnia fits extrapulmonary restriction, such as neuromuscular weakness.

questions.stem: Over the past year he has lost 6 kg although his food intake has not changed. He has no diarrhea, and urinalysis is normal. Which of the following best explains his weight loss?
options: Fat malabsorption from reduced hepatic bile salt secretion
More resting energy spent on the work of breathing
Urinary protein loss from secondary amyloidosis
Reduced intestinal absorption from bowel wall edema
approach: Note the clues: weight loss with normal intake and no gut or kidney losses.
Ask where the extra energy goes: his respiratory muscles work against hyperinflated lungs.
Higher resting energy use, unmatched by intake, burns fat and muscle stores.
questions.why: In severe emphysema, hyperinflation flattens the diaphragm and shortens its fibers, so each breath needs more effort. The respiratory muscles also work against air trapping and raised airway resistance. Their oxygen and energy use at rest is much higher than normal, which raises resting energy expenditure. If intake does not rise to match, the body burns fat and muscle, producing the thin build typical of predominant emphysema. Loss of muscle mass further weakens the respiratory muscles.
whyNot: Mild liver injury does not reduce bile salts enough to cause malabsorption, and he has no diarrhea or steatorrhea.
Correct.
Amyloidosis from chronic inflammation, as in bronchiectasis, causes proteinuria. His urinalysis is normal.
Bowel wall edema can occur with right heart failure, but he has no signs of cor pulmonale or right heart failure.

dx: Acute viral bronchitis in a smoker
case: A 34-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 10-day history of cough. It began with a sore throat and runny nose and was dry at first but now produces small amounts of clear to yellow sputum. She has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 15 years. Temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Lung examination shows scattered rhonchi that clear with coughing. There are no crackles, dullness to percussion, or egophony. A chest x-ray shows no consolidation. Diagnosis: acute viral bronchitis.

questions.stem: Her cough lasts a total of 3 weeks and then resolves without treatment. Which of the following best describes the pathologic process in her lungs during the illness?
options: Fibrinopurulent exudate filling the alveoli of a lobe
Mucous gland hyperplasia of bronchi lasting for years
Transient inflammation of large airway mucosa
Lymphocytic infiltrates widening the alveolar septa
approach: Note the course: a cold followed by cough lasting up to about 3 weeks that clears on its own.
Note the negatives: no crackles, no signs of consolidation, and a clear x-ray, so the alveoli are not involved.
Match this to acute bronchitis, a self-limited inflammation of the trachea and bronchi.
questions.why: Acute bronchitis is inflammation of the trachea and large bronchi, caused by viruses in most cases. Infected epithelium becomes swollen and sheds cells, and mucus production rises, producing cough that can last about 3 weeks. Sputum may turn yellow or green from shed cells and leukocyte enzymes, which does not by itself mean bacterial infection. The alveoli are spared, so there are no signs of consolidation. Chronic bronchitis is a different disease, defined by productive cough for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years.
whyNot: Exudate filling alveoli is pneumonia. It causes crackles, dullness, egophony, and consolidation on x-ray, none of which she has.
Long-standing gland hyperplasia defines chronic bronchitis, with productive cough for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years. Her illness is new and short.
Correct.
Interstitial inflammation of the septa is the pattern of atypical (viral or mycoplasma) pneumonia. It involves the alveolar walls and often shows on x-ray.

questions.stem: The virus infects the epithelium of her trachea and bronchi. Which of the following linings would most likely be seen in a biopsy of the last purely conducting airway, just proximal to the first airway with alveoli opening from its wall?
options: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with many goblet cells
Thin squamous type I cells with scattered cuboidal type II cells
Nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Simple cuboidal epithelium with ciliated cells and club cells
approach: Name the airway: the last purely conducting airway before the respiratory zone is the terminal bronchiole.
Trace the airway lining from the trachea downward: pseudostratified columnar, then simple columnar, then simple cuboidal.
At the terminal bronchioles, the lining is simple cuboidal with some ciliated cells and many club cells, and goblet cells are absent.
questions.why: The trachea and bronchi are lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells, which makes and moves mucus. In the bronchioles the epithelium becomes simple columnar and then simple cuboidal, and goblet cells give way to club cells. Club cells secrete protective proteins, detoxify inhaled chemicals with cytochrome P450 enzymes, and serve as progenitor cells. Beyond the terminal bronchioles, respiratory bronchioles lead to alveoli lined by type I pneumocytes for gas exchange and type II pneumocytes that make surfactant.
whyNot: This lines the trachea and bronchi, the airways infected in acute bronchitis. Goblet cells become scarce in the bronchioles.
Type I and type II pneumocytes line the alveoli, which lie beyond the terminal bronchioles in the respiratory zone.
Stratified squamous epithelium lines the oropharynx and the true vocal folds, where friction is high.
Correct.

topics: Airway epithelium from trachea to alveoli

questions.stem: She asks how continued smoking could lead to emphysema. Which of the following best explains how cigarette smoke shifts the lung toward destruction of alveolar walls?
options: Smoke-induced SERPINA1 mutations that block antitrypsin secretion from liver
Oxidants inactivating antitrypsin as neutrophils release elastase
Nicotine-driven collagen deposition by alveolar fibroblasts
Carbon monoxide inhibition of elastin synthesis by fibroblasts
approach: Recall the normal balance: neutrophil elastase can digest elastin, and alpha-1 antitrypsin inhibits it.
Smoke adds protease: it recruits neutrophils and macrophages that release elastase and other enzymes.
Smoke removes antiprotease: its oxidants inactivate alpha-1 antitrypsin, so elastase acts unopposed.
questions.why: Healthy lung tissue is protected by a balance between proteases, such as neutrophil elastase and macrophage metalloproteinases, and antiproteases, mainly alpha-1 antitrypsin. Cigarette smoke attracts neutrophils and activates macrophages, which raises protease activity. Oxidants in smoke and from activated inflammatory cells oxidize a methionine residue in the active site of alpha-1 antitrypsin, so it can no longer inhibit elastase. With protease activity unchecked, elastin in the alveolar walls is digested, and emphysema develops.
whyNot: Smoke does not mutate the alpha-1 antitrypsin gene in the liver. Inherited mutations cause the deficiency.
Correct.
Collagen deposition causes fibrosis and stiff lungs. Emphysema results from breakdown of elastin, not from excess collagen.
Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin and impairs oxygen delivery. It does not block elastin synthesis.

questions.stem: Which of the following effects of her smoking most increases her risk of developing bacterial pneumonia after this viral illness?
options: Impaired ciliary clearance and alveolar macrophage function
Reduced IgE class switching by B cells in bronchial mucosa
Depletion of CD4+ T cells in bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue
Deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor in the airway lining fluid
approach: List the innate lung defenses: nasal filtering, the mucociliary escalator, cough, secretory IgA, surfactant proteins A and D, and alveolar macrophages.
Ask which ones smoking damages: it slows ciliary beating, causes squamous metaplasia, and impairs macrophage killing.
Add the viral injury: damaged epithelium lets bacteria stick and multiply, so the two insults add up.
questions.why: Most inhaled bacteria never cause infection because innate defenses clear them. Mucus traps particles, and cilia carry it up and out. Secretory IgA blocks attachment, surfactant proteins A and D coat microbes for uptake, and alveolar macrophages ingest and kill what reaches the alveoli. Smoking slows ciliary beating, replaces ciliated cells with squamous cells, and impairs macrophage killing. A viral infection strips ciliated cells further, so a smoker recovering from viral bronchitis is at high risk for bacterial pneumonia. Alcohol, which blunts cough and impairs neutrophils, and inherited ciliary defects raise the risk in similar ways.
whyNot: Correct.
IgE drives allergic reactions and defense against helminths. Less IgE would not raise the risk of bacterial pneumonia.
Smoking does not deplete CD4+ T cells. Profound CD4+ loss occurs in HIV infection.
C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, with swelling episodes rather than pneumonia, and smoking does not cause it.

topics: Effects of smoking on lung defenses

dx: Acute epiglottitis from Haemophilus influenzae type b in an unvaccinated child
case: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 6-hour history of high fever, severe sore throat, and trouble swallowing. He has not received any childhood vaccinations. He is sitting upright, leaning forward with his neck extended, and drooling. His voice is muffled, and he has no cough. Temperature is 39.8 °C (103.6 °F), pulse is 150/min, respirations are 34/min, and blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg. Soft inspiratory stridor is heard. A lateral neck x-ray shows a swollen epiglottis (thumb sign). Blood cultures are obtained. Diagnosis: acute epiglottitis due to Haemophilus influenzae type b.

questions.stem: The physician does not examine his throat with a tongue blade and keeps him sitting upright with a parent while the airway team is called. Which of the following complications is this approach mainly intended to prevent?
options: Complete obstruction of the laryngeal inlet
Aspiration of a pseudomembrane into the trachea
Rupture of a peritonsillar abscess into the airway
Extension of infection into the cavernous sinus
approach: Recognize epiglottitis: sudden fever, drooling, trouble swallowing, muffled voice, tripod posture, and the thumb sign.
Note the anatomy: the swollen epiglottis sits over the laryngeal inlet.
Predict the danger: crying, lying down, or a tongue blade can make the epiglottis close the airway completely.
questions.why: Epiglottitis is a rapidly progressive cellulitis of the epiglottis and nearby supraglottic tissues. In unvaccinated children, Haemophilus influenzae type b is the classic cause. The swollen epiglottis can fall back over the laryngeal inlet, especially when the child lies flat, cries, or has the throat examined, causing sudden complete obstruction. Children lean forward with the neck extended to keep the airway open and drool because swallowing hurts. The airway is secured in a controlled setting before any other procedure.
whyNot: Correct.
A gray pseudomembrane that can come loose and block the airway is a feature of diphtheria, not epiglottitis.
Peritonsillar abscess causes trismus and deviation of the uvula. His swelling is in the epiglottis, not beside the tonsil.
Cavernous sinus thrombosis is a complication of sinus or facial infections. It is not prevented by keeping a child calm and upright.

questions.stem: Before fiberoptic intubation, a topical anesthetic is applied to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds to blunt the cough reflex. Which of the following nerves carries the sensory impulses blocked by this anesthetic?
options: External laryngeal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
approach: Locate the target: laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds.
Recall the division: above the folds, sensation is from the internal laryngeal nerve; below, from the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
The internal laryngeal nerve is the sensory branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, from the vagus.
questions.why: The superior laryngeal nerve, a branch of the vagus, divides into the internal laryngeal nerve, which pierces the thyrohyoid membrane and carries sensation from the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds, and the external laryngeal nerve, which supplies the cricothyroid. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all other intrinsic muscles and the mucosa below the folds. Sensation above the folds triggers the cough that protects the airway. If it is lost, from anesthesia or nerve injury, food and liquid can enter the larynx without a cough, leading to aspiration.
whyNot: The external laryngeal nerve is motor to the cricothyroid muscle, which tenses the vocal folds. It carries no mucosal sensation.
Correct.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies sensation below the vocal folds and all other intrinsic laryngeal muscles.
The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies sensation to the oropharynx and the posterior third of the tongue, and carries the afferent limb of the gag reflex. It does not supply the laryngeal mucosa.

questions.stem: His blood culture grows small gram-negative coccobacilli. Which of the following laboratory features would identify this organism?
options: Growth on charcoal yeast extract agar with cysteine and iron
Large mucoid polysaccharide capsule and lactose fermentation
Oxidase positive with blue-green pigment production
Growth only with both hemin (factor X) and NAD (factor V)
approach: Name the organism from the case: Haemophilus influenzae type b.
Recall its growth needs: factor X (hemin) and factor V (NAD).
Apply them in the lab: it grows on chocolate agar, or on blood agar only next to a Staphylococcus aureus streak (satellite growth).
questions.why: Haemophilus influenzae is a small gram-negative coccobacillus that needs both hemin (factor X) and NAD (factor V). Chocolate agar, made by heating blood to lyse red cells, releases both. On regular blood agar it grows only around colonies of Staphylococcus aureus, which lyse red cells and release NAD. Type b has a polyribosyl ribitol phosphate capsule that resists phagocytosis and causes invasive disease such as epiglottitis and meningitis. The conjugate vaccine against this capsule has made Hib epiglottitis rare.
whyNot: Buffered charcoal yeast extract agar with cysteine and iron is used to grow Legionella, which spreads from contaminated water and causes pneumonia, not epiglottitis.
A thick mucoid capsule and lactose fermentation describe Klebsiella pneumoniae, which causes lobar pneumonia in people with alcohol use disorder.
These features describe Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a cause of pneumonia in people with cystic fibrosis or on ventilators.
Correct.

questions.stem: His narrowed laryngeal inlet raised his airway resistance. In a normal lower respiratory tract, which of the following airway segments contributes the most to total airway resistance?
options: Terminal bronchioles
Alveolar ducts
Medium-sized bronchi
Respiratory bronchioles
approach: Remember that airways branch into many parallel tubes, and parallel resistances combine to a lower total.
Small airways are individually narrow but so many that their combined resistance is low.
Medium-sized bronchi are still few in number and carry fast, often turbulent flow, so they contribute the most.
questions.why: The conducting zone runs from the trachea to the terminal bronchioles and holds about 150 mL of air that takes no part in gas exchange (anatomic dead space). The respiratory zone, from respiratory bronchioles to alveoli, is where gas exchange occurs. Although single small airways are narrow, the total cross-sectional area grows rapidly with each branching, so the combined resistance of small airways is low. Most resistance is in the medium-sized bronchi, where airways are still relatively few and flow is fast and partly turbulent. This is why early small airway disease can be present before spirometry changes much.
whyNot: Each terminal bronchiole is narrow, but there are thousands in parallel, so their combined resistance is low.
Alveolar ducts are part of the respiratory zone. Their combined cross-sectional area is huge, so gas moves mainly by diffusion and resistance is negligible.
Correct.
Respiratory bronchioles begin the respiratory zone. Their total cross-sectional area is very large, so they add little resistance.
